newsitem.title: SPAIN: Communist sees scandals engulfing Spanish politics.
newsitem.headline: Communist sees scandals engulfing Spanish politics.

text.p: The head of Spain's Communist Party predicted a major upheaval in a matter of months, saying scandals from corruption to a "dirty war" on Basque rebels would finally engulf politicians, the police and the army.

Communist chief Julio Anguita, who heads the United Left (IU) group in parliament, accused fellow politicians of being bound by a mafia-like code of silence and said curing what he described as "the gangrene" would be painful and dangerous.
"But we are going to see ourselves undergoing that open-heart surgery within a few months," he told Reuters in an interview late on Tuesday.

Anguita said the turning point would be when Spain's top court decided whether to force conservative Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar to declassify files on the 1983-87 "dirty war" waged under Socialist rule by security forces and hired gunmen.

The documents are sought by courts investigating 28 killings in a campaign of bombings, kidnappings, torture and murder against suspected members of the ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) separatist guerrilla group.
Aznar, who used mounting evidence about this "dirty war" to hound his Socialist predecessor Felipe Gonzalez into holding early elections in March, has so far thwarted the courts.

Now he is in office, he says he is more interested in leading Spain into the future, and especially ensuring it a place in the European Union's planned single currency, than in delving into the past or victimising his predecessor.

"If the Supreme Court tells the government to hand over the files, there will be difficult times in my country," said Anguita, who is often derided by his opponents as a principled fundamentalist out of touch with realities.

"This has many ramifications," he said. "There is pressure ... from corporative structures in the armed forces, the Civil Guard, the national police -- from institutions it's better not to shake too hard because we can come up against great force."
The Communist leader, dubbed "the Red Caliph of Cordoba" after the southern city where he served as mayor early in his career, controls 21 of the 350 seats in the Spanish parliament.

He shocked mainstream parties last month by accusing King Juan Carlos, a living symbol of democracy since the death in 1975 of dictator Francisco Franco, of meddling in politics by backing the drive towards a single currency and entry into NATO's military arm.
Anguita said other parties criticised him for speaking out on corruption and on the "dirty war" because they would prefer to be able to feign surprise when the scandals erupt.

"Logic indicates that the issue of (the anti-ETA drive), the money from secret funds, together with arms- and drugs- trafficking, will blow up one day. And there will be difficult times here in Spain," he said.
"Why are we asked to shut up, United Left and myself? Because they know this is going to happen... my political rivals are betting on the day after tomorrow, when things blow up."
The Supreme Court is to announce before the end of the year whether it wants to question Gonzalez on the anti-ETA drive.

The Socialist leader, who came in a close second in the March election and remains a formidable presence in Spanish politics, denies charges by former subordinates, by Anguita and by Aznar's Popular Party that he oversaw the "dirty war".
His first interior minister and a top Civil Guard general are on trial for setting up and financing the death squads.

The courts are also probing charges that secret interior ministry funds were diverted into private pockets and that the general trafficked in drugs. Socialist Party financing scandals, at national and regional level, are also under investigation.
